lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Antisthenes, Crates — we've got time on our hands. What do you say we take a walk up to the entrance and watch the new arrivals come down? See what they look like, what they're doing.
lines.note: Casual, almost like suggesting a stroll to the corner shop.

lines.speaker: Antisthenes
lines.text: Let's do it. It's quite the spectacle — some of them weeping, some literally begging to be sent back, a few dragging their feet while Hermes shoves them forward by the scruff, digging their heels in and leaning back for all they're worth. For absolutely no reason.
lines.note: Dry relish. The 'for absolutely no reason' lands as the punchline.

lines.speaker: Crates
lines.text: Well, while we're on the subject — I can tell you what I saw on my own way down, if you like.
lines.note: Settling in to tell a story. Warm, conversational.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Go ahead, Crates. You look like a man who witnessed something truly ridiculous.
lines.note: Perfectly flat. He knows exactly what's coming.

lines.speaker: Crates
lines.text: There were quite a few of us coming down together, but the notable ones were Ismenodorus — the rich man, one of ours from home — Arsaces, the viceroy of Media, and Oroites the Armenian. Now, Ismenodorus had been murdered by bandits on Mount Cithaeron, on his way to Eleusis, I think. He was moaning, clutching his wound in both hands, calling out for the children he'd left behind as newborns, and blaming himself for his own recklessness — crossing Cithaeron, traveling through the country around Eleutherae, which is completely desolate because of the wars, and he'd taken only two servants with him. This despite having five gold bowls and four cups on his person.
lines.note: Narrative mode, deadpan. The detail of the crockery is the kicker.

lines.speaker: Crates
lines.text: Arsaces, on the other hand — already quite old, and I must say, not without a certain dignity in his bearing — was furious in that way only barbarians can manage, seething because he had to walk, demanding that his horse be brought to him. And in fact his horse had died with him: a Thracian skirmisher had run them both through with a single thrust at the battle on the Araxes against the Cappadocian. Arsaces had been charging ahead of the others, well in front of the line, and the Thracian — so he told it — ducked under his shield to deflect Arsaces' lance, then leveled his pike and put it through both of them.
lines.note: The battle narrative is delivered briskly, like a military briefing that Crates finds mildly entertaining.

lines.speaker: Antisthenes
lines.text: How is that even possible, Crates? Both of them with one blow?
lines.note: Genuine curiosity. Antisthenes is always the one who asks the technical question.

lines.speaker: Crates
lines.text: Easily enough. Arsaces was charging with a lance about thirty feet long out in front of him. The Thracian knocked the thrust aside with his shield so the point sailed past, then dropped to one knee and received the charge on his pike — wounded the horse under the chest. And the horse, with all that speed and fury, drove itself clean through. Arsaces got it from groin to backside. [pause] You see what happened: it was less the man's achievement than the horse's. Anyway, Arsaces was furious at being ranked with everyone else and insisted he had the right to make the crossing on horseback.
lines.note: 'Less the man's achievement than the horse's' — delivered as a perfectly neutral observation.

lines.speaker: Crates
lines.text: As for Oroites — his feet were completely soft, the man could barely stand on the ground, let alone walk. Which is apparently what happens to all Medes the moment they dismount: they pick their way along on tiptoe as if they're treading on thorns. So when he collapsed and lay there and absolutely refused to get up by any means whatsoever, the excellent Hermes simply picked him up and carried him all the way to the ferry. I was laughing the entire time.
lines.note: 'The excellent Hermes' — utterly ironic. The comedy is in the indignity of a divine psychopomp reduced to carrying a flopped-over nobleman.

lines.speaker: Antisthenes
lines.text: On my own way down, I didn't mingle with the others at all. I left them to their wailing and ran straight for the ferry to get a good seat — make sure I had a comfortable crossing. And while we sailed, they were weeping and seasick, and I was thoroughly enjoying myself at their expense.
lines.note: This is the running gag's pay-off: the austere founder of Cynicism elbowing past the grieving dead to get the window seat. He delivers it without any self-awareness whatsoever.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: So you two had fine company on the road. My travelling companions were Blepsias the moneylender from Pisa, Lampis the Acarnanian mercenary captain, and Damis the rich man from Corinth. Damis had been poisoned by his own son. Lampis had cut his own throat over a courtesan named Myrtium. And Blepsias, the poor wretch, had apparently starved to death — you could tell just by looking at him, pale beyond all reason, thin as you could possibly be.
lines.note: The list is delivered like a roll call. The causes of death are treated with the mild interest of a man reading a ledger.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: I knew how they'd died, of course, but I asked anyway. Then when Damis started blaming his son, I said: 'Well, you can hardly complain — you were sitting on a thousand talents, living in luxury yourself at ninety years old, and you were giving an eighteen-year-old four obols a day.' And to the Acarnanian — he was groaning and cursing Myrtium — I said: 'Who are you blaming Love for? Blame yourself. You never flinched from an enemy in your life, threw yourself into danger ahead of everyone else, and then you were brought down by some cheap little tart and her crocodile tears and stage-managed sighs — you, the brave soldier.' Blepsias, for his part, had already started prosecuting himself before I could get a word in — going on about what a fool he'd been, hoarding his money for heirs who weren't even related to him, the idiot thinking he'd live forever. [pause] But they gave me no small entertainment on the way down, I can tell you.
lines.note: Diogenes is not cruel here — just precise. The comedy is in the accuracy. Each diagnosis lands as self-evident.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Right, we're at the entrance now. We should look out and watch the arrivals from a distance. [pause] Good god, there are so many of them — all sorts — and every single one weeping. Except for the newborns and the very small children. But even the ancient ones are wailing. What is this? Is the love of life really such a grip on them?
lines.note: Diogenes is genuinely puzzled, not contemptuous. The question is almost philosophical.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: I want to ask this one — this extremely ancient one. [to the old man] Why are you weeping, dying at your age? What are you upset about, my friend — you've arrived here as an old man. Were you a king, perhaps?
lines.note: Switching from commentary to direct address. Still completely level.

lines.speaker: The Old Pauper
lines.text: Not at all.
lines.note: Flat. Not even defensive.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: A satrap, then?
lines.note: One notch lower.

lines.speaker: The Old Pauper
lines.text: No.
lines.note: Still flat.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Were you rich, at least? Is that what's painful — leaving all that luxury behind?
lines.note: He's working through the checklist with patient skepticism.

lines.speaker: The Old Pauper
lines.text: Nothing like that. I was about ninety years old. I scraped a living from a fishing rod and a line. Desperately poor. No children. Lame, besides. And my eyesight was nearly gone.
lines.note: No self-pity in the delivery. Just facts. This is what makes it devastating.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: And — being all that — you still wanted to live?
lines.note: Genuine incomprehension, not mockery.

lines.speaker: The Old Pauper
lines.text: Yes. [pause] The light was sweet. Death is terrible. Something to run from.
lines.note: The single most honest line in the collection. No argument, no philosophy. Just the fact of it. Play it quietly.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: You're out of your mind, old man. You're behaving like a teenager in the face of necessity — and you're practically the same age as the ferryman. What is there left to say about young people, when men as old as you are clinging to life like this? You, of all people, should be chasing death as the cure for everything old age has done to you. [pause] Come on, let's go — before someone sees us hovering around the entrance and thinks we're planning an escape.
lines.note: The last line is the comic deflation — the grand philosophical observation undercut by completely mundane self-interest. Exit line, delivered while already walking.
